Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
I try to erase the memory of the event

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
The world is a dangerous place
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a 78-year-old woman whose index trauma is a natural disaster, this trigger is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other triggers, appraisals, memory items, and strategies all fit disaster-related loss/danger themes, but 'being looked at sexually' implies a sexual-threat/sexual-trauma context that is not represented anywhere else in the formulation or item set. This is more than unusual; it introduces a qualitatively different trauma meaning network without supporting items in Threat, Memory, Appraisals, or Strategies.

vignette:
Elena Weber is a 78-year-old graphic designer who has worked from a home studio for years, taking on logo and layout projects for local businesses. She traces the beginning of her difficulties to a hurricane that struck her coastal town three years ago. She and her husband stayed through the storm, believing their house would hold. During the night, the wind changed direction and the back door began slamming against its frame hard enough to shake the walls. Water pushed under the threshold, the power failed, and in the dark she could hear neighboring houses breaking apart. At one point, when they were later taken to a temporary shelter, the sharp smell of spilled rubbing alcohol and liquor from broken containers mixed with wet wood and mildew; she remembers hearing strangers speak in hushed, stunned voices about people who had not been found and families who had lost someone. Those details have remained painfully alive for her.

In the months after, Elena found that ordinary moments could abruptly pull her back into the disaster. If a delivery person let the front door bang shut, or if she heard a heavy door open in the hallway of her apartment building, she would feel a jolt of alarm and think immediately that safety is always temporary, that the world can turn catastrophic without warning. News stories or even casual conversation about someone losing a spouse or child could leave her preoccupied for hours with the conviction that no life is protected from arbitrary devastation. Passing someone who smelled of alcohol in the grocery store or elevator could do the same. Each of these moments seemed to confirm what she had come to believe since the hurricane: the world is dangerous, the basic rules she once trusted have been shattered, and what happened to her and her neighbors was profoundly unfair.

Those beliefs have not stayed abstract. Elena has become consumed with the idea that the catastrophe should somehow have been prevented. She goes over weather reports, evacuation notices, and decisions made by local officials, dwelling on what might have been done differently and what she and her husband should have done sooner. Around the house she repeatedly cleans, straightens, and reorganizes shelves, counters, and her design desk until everything looks controlled and exact. She describes trying to keep disorder from "getting a foothold." She also works hard to push the hurricane out of her mind altogether, cutting off images as soon as they arise and telling herself not to think about it. These habits make sense to her because she is certain that if the world is this unsafe and unjust, she must stay vigilant and keep things under control wherever she can.

Her beliefs also shape the way she remembers the storm. When she speaks about that night, there are moments when the memory does not feel like a memory at all but as if she is back in the blacked-out house hearing the door slam again. At other times she recounts the scene in a flat, distant way, almost puzzled by her own lack of feeling, saying it is like hearing about something that happened to another woman. She often says the whole event feels unreal, too extreme to fit with the life she thought she had. The more she sees the world as permanently dangerous and morally broken, the less the hurricane feels like something completed and placed in the past.

That unstable quality of memory has fed her efforts to manage it. When the scene comes back with a here-and-now force, she starts wiping kitchen surfaces, rearranging drawers, or scrubbing the bathroom grout until her body settles. When the recollection goes numb and unreal, she becomes even more determined to blot it out entirely, as though refusing it might stop it from returning in a more vivid form. Yet over time these strategies seem to have kept the memory both raw and unprocessed. The more forcefully she tries to erase it, the stranger and less fully integrated it feels; the more she relies on cleaning and mental review to contain it, the easier it is for a slamming door or the smell of alcohol to set off the same old surge. Even in her work as a designer, she now keeps her studio door propped open so she will not hear it latch, and she avoids meeting certain clients in person if she thinks she might have to pass through busy office corridors with heavy doors.

By the time Elena sought help, her life had narrowed around these precautions. Her husband had begun commenting that the apartment looked "like a showroom nobody can live in," and she had turned down collaborative projects because she no longer wanted to work in other people's spaces. What finally brought her in was a recent episode when a neighboring apartment door slammed and, for several seconds, she was certain she was back in the storm. Afterward she spent the rest of the day cleaning in silence and that night lay awake thinking again about everything that had not been prevented. She says she is frightened that this is how the rest of her life will be: one sound, one smell, one conversation away from disaster. What she wants most is to feel that the hurricane is over, and that the world, while imperfect, is not about to break open every time a door moves.
